energy. The eruption is still a mystery today in part because the eruption is so brief.

A new research paper published in Geophysical Research Letters shows that the blast was produced by a "super-eruption" — the largest explosion occurring on the Sun's surface. The explosion was the strongest solar flare since the one that hit Earth on July 15, 2002.

"The Sun has been very quiet for a long time," said Dr. John Leinbach, a solar physicist at the Naval Research Lab in Washington, D.C. "This is a surprise, and it's a very important discovery."

The July 15, 2002 flare was caused by a huge eruption of magnetic energy that came from an area on the Sun called the solar corona. The area was heated to millions of degrees and released huge amounts of energy. The eruption created a shock wave that traveled off the surface of the Sun, causing a coronal mass ejection that was directed at Earth.

This article from the Harvard Business Review argues that while many companies are looking to democratize access to data, they’re overlooking the fundamental issue of power and privilege. For example, in the healthcare industry, the patient has the most power when it comes to their data, but healthcare companies have the most power when it comes to treating their patients. If healthcare companies begin to treat the data they collect from patients as an asset, rather than as a liability, patients will be able to benefit from the democratization of data on a much deeper level.

A data democracy is not just about access to data, but about how we use it. We must start from a place of respect for the data and the people who produce it. Data democratization is about giving the power of data back to the people it belongs to.

The shift is a bit of a surprise, since the bike share system has been lauded for its ability to attract tourists to New York City. The bikes are available 24/7, and there’s a special app that allows members to rent bikes with a credit card.

The talks are likely to center on the idea of extending the payroll tax cut, which is paid by both employers and employees and goes to fund the Social Security and Medicare programs.

camera attached to a telescopic pole and a free application on the Internet to make sure householders are not throwing out recyclable materials.
"We're doing this to make people aware of the amount of junk we throw away," said Richard Broome, who has volunteered to document the garbage of five households. "They're usually shocked when they see how much stuff we throw away."

The program, which is being funded by Newcastle University, will also give residents a taste of social networking.

the 2009 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for his discovery of the role of a class of proteins called transcription factors in regulating the expression of genes, will deliver the next Saxon Graham Lecture on Monday, April 16, at 7 p.m. in the Leddy Library Center at the University at Buffalo.
The lecture is free and open to the public. Parking and admission are available at the Buffalo Niagara Convention Center Garage, located at 615 Delaware Ave. on the University at Buffalo campus.
Blumberg is a professor of biochemistry and molecular biology at the University of California, San Francisco (UCSF) and director of the UCSF Institute for Genomic Biology. "This was the No. 1 priority, to remove the corruption that had taken root in the office of the United States attorney," Gonzales said.

Chattanooga, Tenn. (Wade Payne/AP)

When U.S. Attorney General Alberto Gonzales first made his way through a small town in the Deep South, he was on a mission to clean up corruption.

But in his first year on the job, he also drove to a courthouse in one county to sign a sentencing agreement with a corrupt county attorney.

Gonzales, who resigned in 2006 after a political firestorm over the firings of nine U.S. attorneys, was in Chattanooga last month to speak at an event hosted by U.S. Rep. Chuck Fleischmann, R-Tennessee.

Gonzales told the audience of roughly 100 people that his top priority as attorney general was to fight corruption in the U.S. attorney's office.

"This was the No. 1 priority, to remove the corruption that had taken root in the office of the United States attorney," Gonzales said.

Newcastle City Council Mayor Nuatali Nelmes said the speed limit change was a positive move to make the city's streets safer.
"We want to encourage people to walk and cycle around the city, to shop locally and make the city a more enjoyable place to live and work," she said.
"This change will help achieve those goals."
The speed limit was reduced from 80km/h on Hunter Street and Scott Street because of safety concerns.
The local government said "a number of collisions" had occurred on the stretches of road, while pedestrians had been injured.

The first type — the new-to-BI buyer — is in the early stages of adopting BI. These buyers are typically adopting BI to improve decision-making by leveraging data for decision-making.
The second type — the BI-savvy buyer — is an intermediate user of BI. These buyers understand the value of BI but are not yet using it to improve decision-making. These users are likely to be implementing BI projects to support business strategy, such as restructuring a business or improving customer service.
The third type is the advanced user. This is the user who has been using BI for the past three years and is able to provide a detailed history of the project, including recommendations for improving its performance. These users are likely to have already invested in BI tools, which they are using to manage and govern BI
